utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Morrison is away today due to his official engagement. We will be sitting pursuant to 15 bis today. Yes. Good morning, Mr. Tieger. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, General Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We left off yesterday during -- when we were discussing the order that you received from General Mladic via someone at the Main Staff concerning the buses, and I wanted to ask you about one matter that you clarified and -- earlier in your testimony, and that was you had discussed earlier in your Popovic testimony a document that was related to the implementation of this matter that you had originally thought was originated from the secretariat of the Ministry of Defence from Zvornik, but you clarified was a document from the Ministry of Defence sent to Zvornik, and in that connection I wanted to ask you to look at another document, and that would be 65 ter 23640. If we could call that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I had sought leave to add this to the 65 ter list, and there is no objection to that from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It is granted, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, we're still calling up the English, but you should - that's it - see the original in your language. This is a document dated 13 July. It's a report on the mobilisation of vehicles further to your orders, and it provides a list, and it concludes: "Further mobilisation is not possible as all possibilities have been exhausted and passenger transport has been paralysed." And it's signed by Stevan Ivanovic. And if you look at the headers we see at the top, Republika Srpska, Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Defence Zvornik Secretariat, and then the header below or the listing below, Ministry of Defence Pale. And I wanted to ask you, General, if that is an example of -- and further clarifies or eliminates your clarification; that is, that this a document from the ministry -- the Zvornik secretariat to the ministry rather than the other way around?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And is it correct that this is part of the -- is this part of the implementation of the efforts to mobilise buses that was set in motion when you received that phone call in the evening of July 11th?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the time that I received that call and during the following days, the implementation of this activity, in fact, commenced, but here the secretariat of the Ministry of Defence in Zvornik is informing the Ministry of Defence in Pale as you noted, but they are referring to their order, the order of the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska. They're not referring to the Main Staff order, and you noticed that quite correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Understood, and you had contacted the Ministry of Defence pursuant to General Mladic's order asking them to issue such an order to their secretariats; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4552, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I'd like to move on to a meeting that you indicated you had with Mr. Karadzic on the 14th of July, 1995, and some aspects of which you testified about during your Popovic testimony, and I know you also discussed some aspects of that in your Tolimir testimony. At 15484 through 488 in Popovic, you discussed your meeting with the president and Supreme Commander and indicated among other things that you took some documents with you for him to sign; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Among those documents did you -- did you take with you decrees concerning the retirement and/or promotion of certain persons?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Mr. Tieger, I had two decrees with me. One concerned retirement and the other concerned the appointment of two officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And who was the subject of the decree concerning retirement, and who were the subjects of the decrees concerning appointments? And those were -- and tell us, please, the appointments to what positions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decree on retirement concerned General Milenko Zivanovic, and the decree on appointment concerned General Radislav Krstic. He was to be promoted to commander of the Drina Corps. And Colonel Svetozar Andric was to be the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, since, according to the establishment, that is the position of a general. If you appoint a colonel, then the Supreme Commander or the president of the republic is the person who is responsible for such an appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And although I think it's quite clear, just, as you said "if you appoint a colonel," I presume you're indicating if you appoint an officer at the rank of colonel on up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you appoint such an individual to the position of general.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. And so the presentation and signing of those decrees was part of your responsibility and part of the meeting that you had with Mr. Karadzic on the 14th of July; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, let me ask you to look at another document. That's P04485. This is a 13 July 1995 document, General, that I know you've had a chance to see before and specifically during the course of the Tolimir case. It's signed by Radenko Jovicic. Who is General Jovicic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radenko Jovicic was a lieutenant-colonel and he was a personnel officer in the Drina Corps. He was a deputy commander of the command in the Drina Corps for personnel affairs -- or, rather, the assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this document refers to the hand-over of corps commander duties, and it indicates: "Pursuant to the decree of the President of Republika Srpska in the presence of the VRS Main Staff commander Colonel-General Ratko Mladic, the hand-over of the duties of the Drina Corps Commander was carried out on 13 July 1995." And then it refers to the assumption of the post by Major-General Krstic and the appointment of Colonel Andric to the position of corps Chief of Staff and advises that the members of the unit should be informed of that decision in a suitable manner. Can you explain how this relates to the formal signing of the decree or your presentation of the decree to Mr. Karadzic, the president and Supreme Commander, the next day?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to explain this gap in time, this discrepancy. The decree was signed, as you heard, on the 14th of July, and the hand-over of duties took place on the 13th of July. So that was before the decree on these amendments, on these changes, had been issued. I slowed down a little bit, Mr. Tieger, for the sake of the interpreters. I can explain this in the following manner: Lieutenant-Colonel Radenko Jovicic said on the basis of the decree, but you can't see the number. You can see that in the first sentence, because he didn't even know the number of that the decree but he was quite aware of the fact that the decree would be issued. And General Mladic, I assume, certainly knew that the president would sign that decree, which is why that hand-over of duties was, in fact, carried out one day earlier. And I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that it says "forward to." That's beneath the signature, beneath Radenko Jovicic's signature. The document had the following purpose: The brigades of the Drina Corps and the other units, integral parts of the Drina Corps, had to be informed of the fact that there was a change with regard to the corps commander. They should be aware of the fact, and they should know whose orders they were to obey in future.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You mentioned that "General Mladic, I assume, certainly knew that the president would sign the decree," does that mean that you have information about a conversation they had? Does that mean that you know from the nature of the way these matters are required to work that such a conversation must have taken place, or is there another reason why you are certain that General Mladic knew the president would sign the decree?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the proposal for promotions and appointments of generals, the procedure followed was of a somewhat wider, broader nature to collegium sessions attended by commanders from Main Staff. These discussions concerned these proposals and the commanders would make these proposals to the Supreme Commander, to the president of the republic. In the case of Milenko Ivanovic, well, this case was outside the framework of -- that procedure was done outside the framework of that procedure. And I can only assume that General Mladic, and perhaps the Supreme Commander, too, decided to appoint General Krstic as commander. I'm not sure whether they discussed the matter. I assume that they did for sure and that the Supreme Commander accepted the proposal made by the commander of the Main Staff according to which General Krstic should be made corps commander and Milenko Zivanovic should go into retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You referred earlier to Lieutenant-Colonel Jovicic's position as assistant commander in the Drina Corps with a description of -- that seemed to track your own, that is regarding responsibility for personnel. What -- can you just briefly explain what your relationship, professional relationship, was with Lieutenant-Colonel Jovicic was? Was he your subordinate either in a direct manner or along professional lines for reporting and such purposes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Lieutenant-Colonel Radenko Jovicic was directly subordinated to the commander of the Drina Corps. Apart from -- he couldn't do anything without the Drina Corps commander's approval with regard to suggestions, proposals, and so on and so forth, but in professional terms, his duty was to communicate with me. This had to do with technical issues, proposals for promotion, and so on and so forth. If he didn't send a report on time, for example, I could warn him about the fact and tell him that he should act in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you recall Jovicic contacting you or discussion with him the hand-over of duties on the 13th of July; that is, did he abide by his obligation and report to you about this hand-over and the promotion and -- of both Krstic and Andric?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't necessary for him to do that, and it wasn't his duty to inform me of the fact, but let me draw your attention to the word "forward to," Your Honours. You can see that the sector I worked in isn't mentioned. It wasn't forwarded to the Main Staff is what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I'd like to ask you about -- oh, let me, before I leave this subject, ask you to look at another document. That's 65 ter 22824. This is a document from the Republika Srpska press office, dated the 20th of July, 1995, emanating from the cabinet of the president of the republic, and as you can see, it refers to the president of the republic and Supreme Commander of the Republika Srpska armed forces promoting extraordinarily Major-General Zivanovic -- Major-General Krstic to position of the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And praising both Krstic and Zivanovic as architects of the Serbian victories in Srebrenica and Zepa and further reflects the president congratulating the Main Staff, the command of the Drina Corps, and the staff of the police armed forces on the brilliant victory in Srebrenica and Zepa as well as crushing the Muslim offensive in Serbian Sarajevo. And does that communique refer to the same promotion that was the subject of the decree that you took to the president on the 14th and that we've been discussing in connection with the earlier hand-over?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I can remember, and my memory's very reliable in this case, I didn't take the decree on the promotion of Major-General Zivanovic. However, the Supreme Commander has the right to promote even without proposals an officer to the rank of general, to the rank of a general-major or above, and it was customary when a high-ranking officer, when a general, for example, would retire, he would be conferred another rank because he was going into retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that degree of precision, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this document only relates to the extraordinary promotion of Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it's also in reference to the appointment of Major-General Krstic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question -- I'm putting the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, my question is this: When -- when you took the decree or received the decree from the president, was the promotion of General Zivanovic already decided at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So they were related to retirement of General Zivanovic and appointment of General Krstic as the commander of Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it was only at this time that promotion of General Zivanovic was decided. Am I correct in so understanding, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, this document refers to the appointment of General Krstic as the commander of the Drina Corps, which took place already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. But this wording is the sort of wording that was used for the public. The wording is not purely military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger, back to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to clarify one thing, is it your understanding that this document, General, is reporting what has happened up to that date and doesn't necessarily reflect the specific date of the extraordinary promotion of General Zivanovic upon his retirement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, if I could move to a different matter. I'd like you to take a look at 65 ter 00 -- 02275, again a document I know you've seen before. And this is the decision on the proclamation of a state of war in Srebrenica Skelani municipality by the president of the republic, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, dated 14 July 1995. When -- when you became aware either of the pending proclamation of the state of war or the fact that a state of war had been declared in the area on 14 July 1995, did you understand why it was done and why a state of war had been declared on that day in that area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I didn't understand the reasons at the time. I didn't understand why a state of war had only been declared in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you understand why a state of war had only been declared in that area but also on that particular date after -- after the point at which the Bosnian Serb forces had successfully entered and taken control of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to draw your attention to paragraph number 2 where it says: "The aim of proclaiming the state of war is to enable the full engagement of human and material resources in the defence of the republic and final victory over the enemy." Well, that's what perplexes me a bit, to declare a state of war only in part of the territory, and to expect human and material resources to be involved in the entire territory of the republic, that's a bit unclear. And in addition to that, the Main Staff insisted throughout the war that throughout the territory of Republika Srpska a state of war be declared since there was a war going on. That state of war was not declared until 1995. Further on in this document the reasons are explained for declaring a state of war in the municipalities of Srebrenica and Skelani: Paragraph 4, paragraph 5 and 6 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 refers to taking all necessary measures to accomplish the set goals by the organised and effective use of available resources and that to be done in -- by the armed forces in the zone of the Drina Corps. What were the -- General, what were the set goals of the armed forces in the zone of the Drina Corps? And at that time, on July 14th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not recall, Mr. Tieger. I cannot recall these tasks exactly now. If you were to show me a document in order, then I could confirm for you what the tasks actually were. So it wasn't only the Drina Corps that we had in mind. We had six corps and the air force and the PVO, and we in the Main Staff had to deal with all of that. I cannot remember the tasks of each and every individual corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, what was -- what effect did declaring a state of war have on the ability of the army to mobilise both personnel and resources? And let me ask you particularly -- let me ask you that particularly in connection with resources. What did it allow the army to do that it couldn't do before the state of war was declared in connection with civilian assets, resources, equipment, and so on?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, in a state of war, and, now, that is this important distinction, all material and human resources are made available to the military, the armed forces as a whole in order to be able to wage war. And the police as well. It is no longer necessary to submit requests as far as mobilisation is concerned. The economy is also mobilised for war purposes. So all the organs of the state, that is to say the state authorities and the military, use human and material resources in a rational way. Declaring a state of war does not mean that resources should be squandered in any way. They should be used rationally but without any kind of special procedures and requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, so if, for example, the military wanted the use of, for example, civilian -- a civilian bulldozer or civilian excavator, they would now be in a position to obtain that without going through more complicated usual protocols; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. But they have to have a document stating that they had taken it. After all, you cannot take anything away by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I next wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I would tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4553, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, General, I wanted to turn to something that you said in your Popovic testimony concerning the information you received about Srebrenica. At page 15601, you stated that you believe that you personally first heard about the attack on Srebrenica after the war. However, I think you stated something a bit different in Tolimir or tried to clarify that. Can you explain that to the Court, please? And this concerns the subject of when you learned about the attack on Srebrenica and what followed.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tieger, I cannot remember the exact date, but I heard of that activity when the media started talking about that. Your Honours, I would like to point out a methodological problem. Over these past few days and ever since the war ended, I've learned a lot more about Srebrenica than I knew at the time. I also studied some documents in the meantime, too. At that time, I had certain engagement, commitments, then also there was an offensive of Croat and Muslim forces against the western part of the Krajina. So we did not really deal with the problem of Srebrenica in 1995; after the 20th of July 1995, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, General, you indicated that you recall first hearing about Srebrenica when the media started talking about it. Does that mean that you didn't learn about Srebrenica, that is, the fact that the attack had commenced, the fact that it was -- that Bosnian Serb forces had successfully entered Srebrenica, the -- what happened with the population of Srebrenica, and so on, from your fellow members of the staff or from any other members of the VRS during that period of time; that is, during July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tieger. I didn't hear about that. We -- when I say we, it is General Djukic who was sick, and I. We were at the logistics post in Han Pijesak. We were not in contact with our colleagues who were in Crna Rijeka at the main command post. However, as for specific activity, we had that on the 18th of July, 1995. In addition to what I heard through the media, that is when I concluded what it was that was happening in Srebrenica and Zepa, because on the 18th of July, 1995, we had to organise defence of -- of the rear command post in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Either during that general period of time or at any point subsequently, did you ever learn generally or hear generally from your colleagues or other members of the VRS whether the attack on Srebrenica was a -- was essentially a defensive effort to curtail attacks by Muslims from the enclave or was an offensive effort to liberate Srebrenica and bring it within Bosnian Serb authority for all time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, there are several questions here. Could you please be so kind as to break the question up. If not, I have to answer from the point of view of my general knowledge in respect of this question, and that has to do with protected areas and the situation in general from 1994 onwards and the beginning of 1995, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't think the question was unclear, but let me try to make it more clear if -- if that's -- if that wasn't sufficient in the first place. I'm not asking you for your general knowledge or general conclusions. I want to know what you heard from others, from your colleagues. How did they explain, if -- if they explained it to you or alluded to it, what the attack on Srebrenica was about. Was it about curtailing attacks from the enclave, or was it about liberating Srebrenica and bringing it within Bosnian Serb authority for good?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Tieger, but I did not say that the question was unclear to me. I said that it was too extensive and therefore it was hard for me to concentrate. However, Your Honours, after that we did not discuss Srebrenica and Zepa. However, amongst us the belief prevailed that this had been liberation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that connection, let me turn to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. One thing is unclear to me. Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Tieger. You said you knew about Srebrenica only later, after the fall of Srebrenica. Is it related to the attack and fall of -- against and fall of Srebrenica itself, or what issued afterwards? So at -- did you not know that there was an operation against Srebrenica at the time? And you did not know that Srebrenica fell on 11th of July at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly, Your Honour. At the time, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, is it correct that you attended the farewell party or reception for General Zivanovic on the 20th of July at the Jela restaurant?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look quickly at a couple of -- three clips from that, from a video-tape taken of that farewell party. And the first is found at 20 -- 002922, and that's General Mladic speaking, and that is found at page 8 of the hard copy of the transcript in English and page 7 of the hard copy of the transcript in B/C/S. And the 65 ter number is 40206A.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll look at the translation in the hard copy of the English transcript that I'll tender. It indicates, "... who, together" -- excuse me: "You hand over the duty of the commander of the corps to General Krstic, who, together with you, gave the liberated Srebrenica and Zepa to the Serbian people." Next I'd like to turn to comments by General Zivanovic and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- who comments that he's overjoyed because Romanija shines under a Serbian sun and a Serbian beauty. That's at page 12 of the English transcript and page 12 of the B/C/S transcript. And finally, comments by -- excuse me, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, General. Before we move on, if you could quickly ID the persons shown at 00:40:48.2 on the screen in front of you at the moment.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger? Should I start?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left of the screen is General Ratko Mladic. In the middle is General Milenko Zivanovic. He's holding a glass in his hand. And on the right with his arms folded and there's a watch on one of his arms, or on his wrist, that is General Radislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And turning to the last clip, these are comments by General Krstic found at page 13 of the English transcript in -- and page 13 of the B/C/S transcript at the bottom. And these clips are found --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you by any chance not have a hard copy number in compilation of trial video, last four digits?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's not included in the trial video, if that's what you're asking. Did you want the identification number of this transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you referring to this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, he's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have a compilation of transcript. It contains the Jela or this one, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I think I know the transcript you're referring to which is -- I don't think is the Jela transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The index it says, "Part 3, V000-9016, General Milenko Zivanovic's retirement celebration Jela restaurant, ERN V000-4258," is it not? Last page of the index.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm running through that right now to see if the entirety is there, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is explained that origin is the tape provided by Nenad Petrusic, Defence counsel for General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You're right, Mr. President. I don't think these particular clips are contained there, however. I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could move on to the final clip with General Krstic speaking, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And there we -- again, these are the same persons you identified a moment ago; is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And, General, are the clips we've just viewed and the events at the Jela restaurant part of the expression of satisfaction in the liberation of Srebrenica that you referred to a few moments ago in an earlier answer?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that satisfaction was expressed through metaphors that are akin to political speeches rather than anything else. That is my impression, especially General Milenko Zivanovic. He's speaking in metaphors, the sun is shining, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender those clips, and that would conclude my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. They will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4554, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: General, before the other examination begins, there is just one small point I would like you to assist us with. You stated that: "We did not discuss Srebrenica and Zepa. However, amongst us the belief prevailed that they had been liberated." Now, how would you have known this amongst yourselves if there was no discussion? Can you help us there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, as far as I can remember Mr. Tieger's question, he asked me, What was your belief? What had happened to Srebrenica and Zepa? I would put that liberation under quotation marks, you see. We discussed that later, not at that time. I'm talking about ordinary conversations, not official talks. Your Honour, we had constant attacks from the protected areas. Let me not dwell on that subject very long, and that is why I'm putting this word "liberation" under quotation marks. So in ordinary conversations, not official ones, when we talked as human beings, that's how we felt. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. General.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since this is fresh in our minds, perhaps we should start from here and then I'll work -- then we'll work our way backwards. Do you agree that in this situation General Zivanovic does not look surprised or sad because he handed over the corps and because he's retiring?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary, Mr. Karadzic. As a matter of fact, he seems exalted to me. He seems satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were asked about how come it was known that the president would sign this and whether he had spoken to Mladic and so on, do you find this convincing since this was not a surprise to him and it wasn't unpleasant for him in any way? Do you believe that that had already been discussed for quite a while, and do you think that that change had been prepared for quite a while and it wasn't sudden in any way?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I believe, Your Honours, because General Zivanovic had been wounded, and beforehand his retirement had been considered as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that over the last several months General Zivanovic was often on sick leave, was often absent, and that it seemed only natural to all that this replacement would take place? I mean change rather than replacement, because replacement seems to imply degradation.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for pausing as well. This is the first time that we both make pauses without the interpreters asking us to do so. Let me ask you this now: Zivanovic spoke in an exalted way, he spoke in metaphors, and he said that Mount Romanija had the Serb sun shining on it and so on. Do you agree, and the Trial Chamber should know that, that Romanija is not only a legendary Serb mountain, a freedom-loving mountain, and that has to do with the entire period of the Turkish occupation, but at that point in time and before the war it was about 90 per cent Serb populated?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was Serb territory entirely. In certain places there were Muslims as well, but very few of them. Romanija particularly had a glorious history in the Second World War, and there's even a legend about that mountain that has to do with that particular struggle, but let me not go into all that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you've brought Romanija up, do we agree that in the Second World War the commander at Romanija, Slavisa Vajner, was not a Serb and, nevertheless, he had been accepted?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Slavisa Vajner, his nickname was Cica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that at Romanija itself there were about ten Muslim villages that had remained intact because they had surrendered their weapons, and we guarded them, protected them, and fed them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, sorry, I cannot confirm that for you. I really don't know that. I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you don't know if Satorovici and the rest but you may have arrived later. Did you hear that we sent flour to those villages and that we even supplied food to the Croatian villages around Vares? If you weren't present, did you perhaps hear about it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it wasn't only in the case of Romanija but in many locations in the RS where Muslims lived. They received food and everything else, as did other citizens, Mrkonjic Grad, Prijedor, Sanski Most, et cetera. On the basis of such a premise, one can freely conclude that the principle was followed at Romanija as well. As for the other locations I mentioned, I definitely know that Muslims and Croats resided there, and yet those locations were controlled by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that those Muslims and Croats who remained could live freely because they didn't have anyone from their villages in the enemy armies, and those who left were the parents of children who had joined enemy armed forces, and that was the cause of their discomfort.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I know they were safe and they were treated as any other RS citizen. However, I can't tell you for what reasons specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For what reasons some left?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, for what reasons they were safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that there were some festive speeches, and do you agree that the operations around Srebrenica and Zepa were conducted by a single corps and not several? In that regard, the Main Staff did not carry out co-ordination, and perhaps that is why you were unaware of the preparations for that operation.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a corps operation. Even though I still didn't need to know of each and every operation, I was busy with personnel affairs and organisation; hence, I didn't need to take part in all operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I told you that the initial and basic task of the Drina Corps was to separate the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica and to free up the road between Milici and Skelani, which should not have been cut off in the first place, is it possible that this was so without you being aware of the preparations and the task itself?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible it was so, Mr. Karadzic, but it is also possible that no one needed to inform me. Besides, I saw many documents after the war, including here at the Tribunal where I could conclude that the task was to separate the enclaves rather than occupy them. I also saw a document by which you approved that the operation continue, although it had not been originally issued as a task to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us be precise. What does liberation mean? Do we agree that later on it was seen as a process of liberation, although it had not been the original task?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw that I sort of praised General Krstic, which didn't help him much before this Tribunal. Do you agree that that, too, was a political gesture on my part so that the fame would be distributed across all in the field and that not all be ascribed to Mladic alone?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. I also learned about that from a book written by Dr. Kosta Cavoski. I saw a document, too, where you state that General Mladic was a living legend because we turned him into one but there were other generals who need to take the praise, which included General Krstic. Perhaps I did not quote you directly. It's a paraphrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you D2058 in e-court. While we are waiting for the document, General, you confirmed that on the 18th, you had to organise the defence of the Main Staff area and the area of the logistics base. Who were you defending the area from when Srebrenica was liberated on the 11th and 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were defending the rear command post in Han Pijesak. It was attacked by armed Muslim groups which were the leftover parts of the 28th Division of Army -- of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which used to have its command post in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you were asked about the reasons for the proclamation of the state of war -- well, this seems not to be the right document. D2058. When you were asked about the reasons why war was proclaimed in that area, by virtue of your position in the Main Staff you did not need to be aware of such reasons.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the whole of the Main Staff, and my sector in particular, it was very important that the war had been proclaimed. Now, why, that is something we were not interested in. It was a particular situation, a particular social process which enabled us to carry out certain military activities, and we could do it more easily than without the war being proclaimed as I have explained Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you did not object, because the army wanted the war proclaimed as of the moment the Muslim side declared war on us in 1992. In this fashion, you -- you could more easily defend yourselves, and you could use the situation of the war proclamation until the Muslims stopped waging war on us.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We didn't hear the witness's answer. "Precisely" is your answer, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I was going to ask for a citation of the particular document. I presume this is a reference to a document declaring a state of war but one which suggests that the document is directed at -- at a particular other party. It's a nuanced distinction but one the accused continues to make, and I think it is an inaccurate reflection of what I believe he is actually referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I was about to ask the time-frame. In the question, Mr. Karadzic said: "... because the army wanted the war proclaimed as of the moment the Muslim side declared war on us in 1992." Did you mean that despite such wishes of the military, Mr. Karadzic did not proclaim the war until this time? Is it what you said, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the army demanded and wanted that war be declared, but the president of the republic -- I'm sorry, I hope I'm not too loud. But the president of the republic who could do so would not until this date, on the 14th of July 1995, and only in one part of RS territory, in the municipalities of Skelani and Srebrenica. As for the whole of the RS territory, a state of war was proclaimed only as late as July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was there any part of the territory as -- as to which the proclamation of war was declared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In the territory of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, which is the area around Sarajevo. I think it was on the 23rd of July, 1995, that the state of war was declared there. I apologise if I'm mistaken about the date. It also included the area of the 2nd Krajina Corps in the area of Drvar and in the western part of RS. It was sometime in mid-1994 or in the second half of 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me be of assistance -- well, I'll ask you to assist. Do you agree that we declared a state of war in certain areas only under extraordinary circumstances, when all elements of the society needed to be included so as to defend it, that is to say, when we were on the brink of defeat?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. You assessed the situation, and you declared the state of war by virtue of decrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Although we still have not seen the minutes of the Rump Presidency session of Bosnia-Herzegovina, do we agree that the Muslim side declared war on us on the 20th of June, 1992, and that it actually took place as of the 22nd of June? By having done so, they turned Bosnia into a theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that it happened even before that date. As a member of the JNA, I was in charge of analysing the situation across SFRY territory. We established that President Alija Izetbegovic, although he was the president of Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina in April 1992, renamed the republican TO staff into the TO staff of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the 8th of April, 1992, he declared the state of an imminent threat of war, which meant that the war was imminent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that on the 8th of April, he removed General Vukosavljevic and appointed Hasanefendic, following which there were a number of directives against the JNA and Serbs in the Serb autonomous districts?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. I only want to add that in all such documents the JNA and Serbs were termed the aggressor. However, they did not use the term "Serbs" but "Chetniks."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you cast a glance on this document from the State Security Service, informing that on the 14th in the area of Pobudje, the municipality of Bratunac, 5.000 group strong was spotted, and out of the 5.000, 500 were armed. Do you agree that on the 11th the Serb army only entered Srebrenica, whereas the 28th Division was in the forests. It was only on the 16th that 10.000 fighters, as the Muslims reported, broke through to Tuzla. Until the 16th, they were scattered in the forests, presenting a grave danger to the Serbs in both villages and towns?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I did not follow such activities. I can neither deny nor confirm your assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you did know that you had to defend the rear command post as it was under threat from these groups. It was following the 14th, as late as the 18th; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course there was an armed conflict. There was a clash as well in Mokro village, which is between Han Pijesak and Sokolac. We clashed with those groups. How many were there? Well, many, and they kept moving back and forth between Srebrenica and Zepa towards Kladanj and Olovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I told you that representatives of the civilian authorities of Bratunac and Srebrenica on the 14th asked me to declare the state of war as they were unable to guarantee their survival if those units turned on them, would you then conclude that that was the reason why the entire 28th Division, 10- to 15.000 soldiers -- could you accept that as the reason for the declaration of the state of war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the witness said he didn't know. I don't see the point of further pursuing that issue with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, esteemed Mr. Tieger is trying to say that we needed to militarise the area of the Drina Corps so that the army could mobilise some excavators in an easier way. Does this sound justified, reasonable, or is it simply far-fetched?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he answered the question. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think you're right, Mr. President, not to mention that that's a mischaracterisation of the colloquy that took place during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He said he did not know the reason or he was not interested. You have another opportunity to -- as to the reason for that proclamation, but move on with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that you answered this already, how decrees are passed. Do you agree that rarely, or practically never, I would promote someone, especially I never demoted anyone, apart from the proposals that would come from the professional and command structures of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Mr. Karadzic. As president of the republic, you adopted our proposals -- or, rather, proposals of the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, General Mladic, who made decisions on the basis of consultations with us in the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday there was mention of the time when you received General Mladic's order to take care of buses. Did you notice that for the learned Mr. Tieger the time itself was important, when this happened, at what time in the evening on the 11th. So let me ask you then: Is it correct that in our zone summer-time is one hour ahead, just like in Europe?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that in that area, especially up there in the mountains, it would get dark considerably later, that the day was quite long?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the geographical situation. It's not that the sun would set very early.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When General Mladic ordered you to take care of -- or, rather, issue orders for the mobilisation of buses, did he tell you that he did that after some meeting, after some meeting with Karremans; or for example, did he tell you that Karremans had conveyed a request by General Nikolai to have the Army of Republika Srpska assist in the evacuation? Did you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I had already answered that General Mladic did not talk to me at all. His order was conveyed to me without any kind of further explanation. It was clear to me how I was supposed to act, and that is what I answered a few minutes ago or perhaps yesterday. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, there was a bit of hair splitting as to whether it was late at night. Is it possible that this was conveyed to you considerably after 8.00, and in that area there was still visibility at that point in time? Was that before nightfall, actually?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karadzic, I cannot remember exactly. I know for sure that it was in the early evening. I would not like to retract the answer that I've already given. I am sorry, Your Honours, but it didn't really matter to me then what time it was, and don't that so well. It was the task that mattered to me, not the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, but yesterday at first you said late in the evening -- late at night, rather, and then Mr. Tieger tried to make it as early as possible. Do you allow for the possibility that it was considerably after 2000 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like a transcript reference for that. That's not the way I remember the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us take a look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is page 74, page 75 yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you refer to the summary Mr. Tieger read out?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think that the questions had already started, and the General was asked when it was that he received this task on the 11th, and the General said, "Late at night."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's page 79 para -- line 21: "Q. ... can you tell us approximately when you received it on July 11th?" "A. As far as I remember, it was late in the evening that I received the phone call." And then, referring to Tolimir probably: "Q. ... let me ask you for some clarification on that. I know at page 18731 of your testimony in the Tolimir case, you referred to the afternoon and then most probably the evening hours. So is it correct we're talking about sometime ... not necessarily afternoon, but sometime around evening?" "A. Yes. That was a better way to put it."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and if I may say, this is one more in an amazingly lengthy series of misrepresentations. I don't remember any reference to night. So now Dr. Karadzic tries to change it from references to the evening to references at night and tries to act as if that's part of the witness's previous answer. That's very unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Late in the evening. I read out the entire passage. Let us move on. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, my question -- or, rather, my clarification was the following: When we say late in the evening, that does not mean evening. It does -- we say late in the evening even when we refer to night-time. Evening is all the way up to midnight. You can check that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are not giving evidence. If you like, you could do so. Instead of making statements, put your question to the witness, and I think the witness answered -- has answered the question already. I see the time, so put your question if you like with respect to the time, and we'll take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, when we say "late in the evening" in our language, is there a restriction involved, or does late evening mean that night had already fallen and that it is already night-time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, late in the evening, that means at dusk. I would not want to change my earlier answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dusk in our part of the world is after 8.00; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Since it was summer-time by then, it was after 8.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you confirm whether it is true that the buses were only mobilised in Republika Srpska, or were they mobilised somewhere else as well?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were only mobilised in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 73 of yesterday's transcript, you corrected something that was said in a question, namely that Ratko Mladic wasn't the chief but, rather, the commander of the Main Staff. Why did you make that correction, and is it of any significance?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, according to the establishment position, it's not the chief but the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS as a personnel officer. It was my duty to draw your attention to the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So is there a difference, a substantial difference, between the post of chief and the post of commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of the Main Staff is someone who is in charge of the army, whereas the commander exercises command over the army. Their duties are similar, and there is no substantial difference. The difference is just a terminological difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One leads and the other commands. The commander exercises command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to ask you the following: Is it correct that before the war you worked in the administration for morale, in the Federal Ministry of People's Defence, the Federal Secretariat for National Defence is what we called it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you occupied that position, did you have the opportunity to obtain information and to follow the events that concerned politics and events that related to security and, in particular, army security?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We followed the information, in particular through the media. We followed information that had to do with the JNA and the All People's Defence, and from that administration there were people who participated in expert teams from the JNA General Staff, and these teams had to do with analysing the security situation in the territory of the entire Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, the territory of the SFRY, which is the abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that you also took into consideration political movements, the appearance of political parties, political phenomena? Did you analyse this from the point of view of how these things might have an influence on the security of the country and on the role the army was to play?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We analysed social processes in particular. As for political processes and activities of the political parties that appeared at the time once the multi-party system had been introduced into the SFRY, we included an analysis of these things through -- or, rather, in our analysis of the social processes that we were following.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. So do we then agree that from the outset the JNA from -- from the outset of the crisis and up until the withdrawal from Bosnia and Herzegovina and Macedonia, the JNA, in accordance with the constitution, wanted to preserve the integrity, the territorial integrity, and unity of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Its main purpose is defined by the constitution and by the law on the armed forces. Its main role was to confront an external aggressor. The entire system that involved preparing for defence was guided by that main task. It was not prepared for armed conflicts within the SFRY. You correctly defined its constitutional task. Your Honours, we officers took an oath when we joined the service. According to the oath, we said, I - I'm paraphrasing - hereby solemnly undertake to preserve the integrity and the sovereignty of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and so on and so forth, I will obey the orders issued by my officers, et cetera. I don't want to tell you what the oath consisted of in its entirety off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, is it correct that the previous system of All People's Defence and social self-protection together with its territorial units and together with the various levels that were responsible for defence and that goes from republics through municipalities, to local communes, to companies, is it true that the entire system at one point in time proved to be a good basis for the development of paramilitary formations, republican armies, and was it something that in the end threatened the unit of the country?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already mentioned the law on the armed forces, and according to that law the armed forces consisted of the JNA, the Territorial Defence, and the police in wartime. They all received weapons on the basis of the concept of All People's Defence, which can be summarised as follows: Every citizen is a soldier. Every soldier is a citizen. And the JNA and the Territorial Defence had weapons at their disposal together with a certain amount of ammunition. So the assumption that these groups could have armed themselves in this way is not a groundless assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I assist the interpreters. When you said several bks, does that mean several combat sets, and what sort of an amount of ammunition does this involve when you refer to a combat set?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the abbreviation bk means combat sets, so you're quite correct. Every individual soldier had one and a half combat sets for his personal use and for artillery pieces, and so on and so forth. One combat set would be issued. In the wartime reserves there were two combat sets for every combatant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that the SFRY Presidency, prior to the multi-party elections, tried to repair the damage done, and they wanted all these weapons to be monitored by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and I do think that there are documents to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that it was on this basis that paramilitary formations started appearing as well as republican armies, first of all in Slovenia and Croatia, and they consisted of Territorial Defence units, they consisted of police units, strengthened police units from the reserve forces, and also they consisted of units that were the Guards or the Patriotic League in Bosnia, the Green Berets? They were outside of official structures. Is it true that the national secretariat for federal defence had to confront an enemy that wasn't an external enemy but was an internal enemy, and that enemy's military capacity was increasing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd just like to point something out for your benefit. The Presidency of the SFRY and the JNA and its General Staff in particular didn't consider the Territorial Defence in Slovenia to be a paramilitary formation, because the Territorial Defence in Slovenia was an entity that existed pursuant to the law. It was an integral part of the armed forces. But the Territorial Defence in Slovenia launched an attack on the JNA. As for everything else that you said, Mr. Karadzic, well, yes, all these other elements that you mentioned, Mr. Karadzic, were considered to be paramilitary formations by the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that you did have insight into what was happening in the JNA in those two republics, and can we agree that soldiers, officers, and their families, the equipment that they had at their disposal were under threat, under blockade, so they had been placed in an impossible situation, to be brief.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the administration where I worked, we had a very good overview of the situation, and we conducted an analysis on the way in which the overall situation influenced the morale in the army. We drew the following conclusions. The consequences suffered were traumatic, the consequences suffered by officers and soldiers. The soldiers were recruits who were 19 to 20 years old. They would be attacked. The electricity supply and water supply would be cut off. They wouldn't be provided with water. In Zagreb, officers complained to me. They said their neighbours were threatening them and they had to move out. I also spoke to a doctor in Zagreb - this was in 1991 - and he told me, Colonel, the officers are very afraid. They are afraid for their families, and some of them started moving out. They started moving their families out, in fact. They moved them to other parts of the territory. That was the situation in Slovenia. That's where everything started, and then it continued in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm wondering how much this line of questioning will assist you for your defence. Could you not be more succinct on your cross-examination as regards the matters that were not dealt with in examination-in-chief? Just for planning purpose, how much longer would you need for your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think I've been allocated two and a half hours. I've used up half an hour. I used up half an hour in the first session. I have another two hours, and I will complete my cross-examination within the time allocated to me, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Allotted time always means up to that hours. You don't have to right -- you don't have to use them all. If you can finish before then, it's much better. Please move on, Mr. Karadzic, but please focus on more critical issues to your defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency, but when listening to the Prosecution in the Seselj case, I'm surprised. It was as if there hadn't been a war, as if the Serbs suddenly launched an attack on other peoples. So I want to establish the basis to see what was actually happening. Were we savages who just decided to attack our neighbours, or did something happen which is why the situation developed in the way that it? These are why these things are important for me because the General occupied a position from which he could observe everything, but I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said today that you also followed new political developments. Do you agree that there were new parties that appeared, especially in Croatia, and these parties had rhetoric that was frightening for the Serbs? They also had symbols from the Second World War, flags, coats of arms, and a particular kind of rhetoric that they would use which the Serbs found frightening?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were symbols and a certain type of rhetoric in speeches, and this showed everyone that the Serbs were in danger in that territory. The survival of the Serbs was under threat. And these things could be noticed amongst members of the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Party, which was established, I think, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, did you in Bosnia-Herzegovina know -- in the Federal Secretariat for All People's Defence, did you know that there were new parties that were being established and were you familiar with their programmes and rhetoric that they used, as well as the way in which they conducted themselves?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we followed such events as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the Serbian Democratic Party was one of the last national parties to be established, and I appeared on the political scene -- well, I was someone who appeared at the later stage on the political scene?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, according to the information we had at that time, yes, that's correct. At the beginning -- I apologise to you, but at the beginning we didn't really pay much attention to that party or to you personally. You didn't say anything against the JNA in your speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that in Croatia the formation of paramilitaries was undertaken by the state itself, and the only political party that had its own paramilitary formation was the SDA in Bosnia-Herzegovina? The formation was called the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we forwarded our conclusions to the Federal Secretary for National Defence, to General Veljko Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that following Hitler it was probably the first political party to have its party army?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether you can put it in such world context, but in any case, in our part of the world it's the first party that had a political armed force, and specifically I have in mind Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the media there was this anti-Yugoslav, anti-Serb as well as anti-army campaign? Despite many contacts with the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and many agreements on the role of the JNA, the media portrayed it quite differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I hesitate to rise on matters of this type, but if the accused is going to pursue them then I guess I have an obligation to ask for some precision to the question here is whether the accused is asking about one particular type of alleged media coverage and conflating them all; that is, anti-army is anti-Serb is anti-Yugoslav, etc cetera, or if he's asking about three or four separate kinds of media approaches. And if it's the latter he should separate them, and if it's the former, he should first ask if there is a basis in the witness's assessment for lumping them together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, even if answered in a positive matter, general statements do not help the Chamber at all. Be specific. And I would urge you to move on to more critical issues. Save your energy. We have a lot in our adjudicated facts. I do not look into those at this moment, and there are various ways for you to tender the background history. You don't have to put every aspect of background to every witness. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Even with utmost respect, I must say that it is my understanding of the indictment that I was accused or charged with the creation of policy which resulted in the events we are familiar with, and it is our position that we merely responded to the actions of others. This General at the time was positioned in the Ministry of Defence of Yugoslavia. He held such a position which was in charge of assessing the impact of media reporting on inciting military conflict and nobody can address the influence of the media in Bosnia better than this witness and the effect it had on the undermining of the country as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll cut it short, General. Did you in the Federal Ministry of National Defence have concerns about the conduct or media reporting in Bosnia-Herzegovina and its impact on inter-ethnic relations and the stability of the country?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. We were gravely concerned following the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We proposed our conclusions to the General, stating that should that situation continue, a result would be a bloody war. We presented it to him by way of a model, and we reminded him of the war in Lebanon which had a similar civil war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were your concerns raised because you seemed to have viewed Bosnia and Herzegovina as a potential powder keg?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, Mr. Karadzic. I believe we even used that very phrase in a number of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, since I was not of any interest to you, do you agree that no Radovan Karadzic could manipulate or incite the Serb people given the fact that those people had fresh memories of the genocide of 1941? Were you able to observe that -- whether my conduct was aimed at manipulating and inciting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I can only address your thesis of genocide. As for the rest of your question, I'd rather not comment. No person, including Karadzic or Raskovic or anyone, needed to tell the people of the dangers of genocide. The Serb people were well aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to notice that on behalf of my party and my ethnic community, I proposed peaceful political solutions and that I did my utmost to avoid the conflict? Was it the extent of your knowledge concerning my activities in the Federal Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such parts as were reported by the media or broadcast, that is what we followed, including your statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From the point of view of security of the state and the preservation of its unity, was there anything in my political position that would be of concerning to you in the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, Mr. Karadzic, I don't recall having reached such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it your belief that the danger for Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina was a realistic one and that in Bosnia they would have suffered had they not defended themselves?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You put it precisely. It was a belief which is part of our thinking process and figures as fact, and the fact of this fear of the Serb people was based on their historical experience, especially in World War II and the contemporaneous political statements, in particular made by Franjo Tudjman, Croatian president, who divided Serbs into three categories, and I'll paraphrase: One-third of the Serbs need to be killed, another third driven out, and the last third, if they remained in Croatian territory, should be converted to Catholicism. A month ago, President Mesic, former Croatian president, in his discussion with the RS president asked, What is Dodik going to do now? Dodik is the current RS president. If there's another war, Republika Srpska will disappear, as will the Serbs. Your Honour, I did not discuss the historical reasons which clearly indicate the danger of genocide, and you may well be aware of some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Do you remember that this Mr. Mesic, in 1991, on several occasions warned against the spill-over of war from Croatia into Bosnia, and indeed it came true, thus easing the position of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honours. I would remind you of a very stringent statement made by that gentleman. He went to the Croatian parliament, and he said, I have completed my task. Yugoslavia is no more. And yet he had been a member of the Yugoslav Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And for a period of time he was even the president of that Presidency, and he swore to preserve that very Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you follow the attempts in Bosnia-Herzegovina made at trying to avoid the war and to use the JNA to put a stop to the conflict and separate the parties at Izetbegovic's request as well as at the request of other BiH Presidency members?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such attempts. The JNA General Staff believed that the JNA should play a buffer role in order to prevent interethnic conflict. However, they failed in Croatia, and we were quite weary of using that idea in Bosnia-Herzegovina as we were not convinced it would work. Your Honours, I no longer recall if it was in 1991, but I went to Bosnia and Herzegovina as part of a General Staff team. The intention was to see what the situation was like, and I was particularly tasked with morale issues. I was quite pleased to see that there were joint police patrols together with members of the JNA, but it only lasted for a short time because the same formations which had patrolled together clashed later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you this: Were you privy or did you follow the international conference on Yugoslavia, especially its sub-conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina chaired by Lord Carrington and Ambassador Cutileiro?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We followed those developments starting with Lisbon through Paris, Vienna, and other locations. There were different rounds of talks. And all those commissions, starting with Vance-Owen and then Stoltenberg and other UN representatives, it is -- it was all followed. I can also tell you, Your Honours, that we appreciated their efforts in achieving peace so as to avoid this bloodshed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was the view of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
