utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like us to move on to the outbreak of war. You did not immediately join the VRS, but you are aware of its formation, establishment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I do scientific work and write articles for the encyclopedia, and part of my entries concern Republika Srpska; therefore, I am quite familiar with this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do we agree that other ethnic communities, perhaps not in Macedonia but in the runaway republics, quite early on pulled out their command cadre and reserve force as well as conscripts from the JNA, thus establishing their republican armies? Everyone had done that before the Serbs in Bosnia did the same.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a historical fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that the weapons and assets, as well as equipment available to the ethnic communities, was confiscated right away, taken over and put to use, and this included warehouses, ammunition and weapons factories, depots of the TO, et cetera? Was it all unilaterally taken wherever it was available and then distributed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. And not only that. They even received weapons of different types, even heavy weaponry and missiles from abroad. I'd like to remind you of the Kikas affair, Your Honours. Kikas is a heavy-duty transport aeroplane for civilian use. It was forced it land in Zagreb. It belonged to the JNA. It had flown in from Uganda and was packed with weapons. Then there was the Cazmatrans affair. General Martin Spegelj was tried and convicted of importing weapons from Hungary. They had TO assets at their disposal as well as JNA items from warehouses, and on top of it all they procured weapons from abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Since most of it was known to the public, do we agree that the Serb side was very disappointed and upset when it realised that the JNA was to take up a neutral position and that the Serb side expected the Yugoslav state and its institutions to protect our right to remain within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it wasn't only the politicians who were disappointed. I think the Serbs as a whole were disappointed in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So do we agree that the Serbian people were angry for a long time with the Yugoslav People's Army? And when the JNA withdrew, the Serbian people suddenly had an army, whereas the other communities gradually formed an army from that very same JNA. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's several questions there, Mr. Karadzic. First of all, yes, the people really were very angry. As an officer, it was very unpleasant to speak to the people when people would say, What are you doing? Are the people going to be killed? And you are withdrawing. Secondly, weapons were not only obtained from the JNA, because the JNA withdrew with its weapons, to a large extent. They withdrew from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina with their weapons, but many weapons arrived from Slovenia and Croatia. That is a fact. Most of the weapons were obtained by everyone from the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let me ask you this: When the Yugoslav People's Army moves its reserves of weapons and artillery pieces to the Serbian areas, did they want to arm the Serbs, or did they want to ensure that they could defend themselves from attacks? Did they want to prevent this equipment from being taken in territories where people were not in favour of the JNA? Did they act in this way for their own sake or for the sake of the local Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For their own sake, Mr. Karadzic, in territory under the control of Serbs. That territory was the safest territory, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The time that the VRS was established, our law referred to a slightly unusual organisation, because our General Staff was called the Main Staff. Do you agree that this was somewhat unusual, and why?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is usual in the case of all armies through -- throughout the world that the term is the Chief of the General Staff. I think that is the case in the east and in the west. This term, the commander of the Main Staff, is a little unusual, but it has a historical background. There are historical reasons, establishment reasons for the use of this term. The establish reasons are that there was the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo, and pursuant to a degree from the president of the SFRY, Ratko Mladic was at the head of that military district. So there was the commander who headed that military district. And throughout the territory of the SFRY there were commanders in those stretches of territory and not Chiefs of General Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it your position that the armed forces -- a complex organisation, and the Supreme Commander of the armed forces is the president of the republic ex officio, and the armed forces are unified only in -- under wartime conditions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So do we agree that either the commander or the Chief of Staff has command over the army, whereas it's the minister of the interior or his commander who has command over the police? At the strategic level in the case of war, if war is declared, the president plays the role of the Supreme Commander of the unified armed forces.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Karadzic. Were you asking me what the situation was in the case of war or state of war?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To say state of war is probably more correct.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is a state of war, the supreme commanders -- the Supreme Commander is the commander of all those who are armed in the state, in the republic. So that concerns the police and the army. But regardless of the state of war, the Supreme Commander doesn't lose his role. It consists of exercising command over the army, and that is the case in wartime and in peacetime. Your Honours, you saw the responsibility of the president in the decrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So do we agree that when you referred to the responsibilities of the president of the republic, the president of the republic could command in strategic terms. The president of the republic couldn't have direct control over the army without acting through the Main Staff and its commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Is that a question asking for an interpretation of the operative law or principles or asking for the de facto possibilities and realities of what the president of the republic could or did do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that the question can be put, and if necessary, you can take up the issue in your re-examination, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand, but let me just note that the accused just went into about 45 minutes, if not longer, of basically evidence that is intended to aid his own case. It didn't arise from the cross-examination [sic]. And once again, as in many occasions in the past, the Prosecution is obliged to either conduct what's essentially a cross-examination that takes time out of the allotment for our own case and that I don't think was intended for that process or to forego cross-examination. So we are always presented with the dilemma, which is why I rise, to get as much clarity during the course of the cross-examination as possible so that at least we minimise the impact of that problem when possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's proceed, Mr. Karadzic. Now, General, can you answer the question whether the president of the republic could not have direct control over the army without acting through the Main Staff and its commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As a general, he could order or monitor and control through the Main Staff, but he can directly order to the commander of a corps, can he not? And the commander of the Drina Corps or Sarajevo Corps, Eastern Bosnia Corps can report to the Main Staff. That's envisaged, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you referred to the president as general - that's the interpretation I received - but he doesn't have a rank, so I apologise for drawing your attention to that. But if the president contacted corps commanders, he is not by-passing the provisions. That is his prerogative. But the corps commander has the responsibility of informing the commander of the Main Staff about the fact that the president contacted him and the reasons for which this was done. For example, if the president contacted me as the Supreme Commander -- he didn't do that, but if he had done that and had told me something, I would have had to report it to the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, General Mladic, and I would have had to inform him of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So that Mr. Tieger is also satisfied, I'll put a concrete question to you now. Did you notice that I was dissatisfied with the level of control and the level of influence exercised over the army?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karadzic, I don't really understand your question, because there are various ways of exercising control. The Ministry of Defence, for example, conducts controls that relate to inspection. Within the army, you control combat readiness. Please don't bear grudge against me for not having understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll be even more concrete. Do we agree that there were significant cases in which there was suspicion on the part of the civilian authorities. The commanding officers were also suspicious of certain ideological matters. There was suspicion aroused for ideological reasons. Can we agree about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it wasn't just a lack of trust. It's not just a matter of these suspicions. There were differences as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that there was tension between the civilian authorities, and in particular between me and the Main Staff, and this was for various reasons? For example, was one of the reasons that I was saying that too many people were being taken from their jobs in the economy, and, as a result, the economy wasn't functioning properly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a continual objection of yours that you levelled at the army. You said that they were megalomaniacs in their requests, and this is something that you would practically say at all the meetings of the Supreme Command, all the meetings that I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that I tried to exercise more influence on the army, i.e., through the ministry or in direct terms? I didn't really believe that I knew everything, nor did I believe that I could have control over everything. In fact, did I try to exercise command, and was I unsuccessful in my attempts?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there are several examples of you making such attempts, Mr. President, but in some of the cases you weren't successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that I couldn't transform the General Staff into the Main Staff [as interpreted], and I couldn't replace the first person in charge because he was appointed by the Assembly and only the Assembly could replace that person?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I indirectly found out that the president wanted to replace Mladic in 1993, but I was the direct witness of the fact that the president established some sort of a defence council and he appointed General Mladic to that position, and in Main Staff of the VRS, we took this to be a replacement. So the president replaced Mladic on the 4th of August, 1995, and we had a collegium session of the Main Staff of the VRS that almost all of us attended. That was on the 6th or the 8th of August. I apologise if I said July. It was on the 6th or the 8th of August, several days after that replacement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber how the collegium of generals acted in relation to that decision that I took?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that we were familiar with the legal provisions that governed that issue, we wrote a letter that we all signed, and we suggested that the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska should not accept the replacement of General Mladic. We suggested that he remain the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, and we were aware of the fact that at the time the president did not even have the right to replace General Mladic or to appoint him to a different position. And we took this appointment to be a matter of replacement, because appointing Ratko Mladic as commander of the Main Staff was done by the people's Assembly in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Previous page of the transcript, lines from 16 to 18. It's from your question, so I wonder whether that's a translation issue or whether -- or it's correct. You are recorded having asked like this: "Is it true that I couldn't transform the General Staff into the Main Staff ..." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Vice versa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It should be the other way around.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: The other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in the meantime, I wonder whether you can try to conclude your cross-examination by the end of this session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another half hour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, half an hour from now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it the total of allocated time I have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. You will have about 25 minutes in the next session, but I'm just asking whether it is possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Excellencies, I'd much rather use up the whole time, because rarely do we have a person such as this who was intimately familiar with the personnel structure of the VRS, but I'll rush ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, could we look at 1D5168. I believe it has been admitted. Is this a document you drafted and signed that was sent to the state Assembly and the republican president concerning my attempt to rename the General Staff to Main Staff and to involve Mladic in politics so as to appoint him as the head of council?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 2 and 3 for the General so he can see the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, tell us when to go to page 3.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this some sort of petition, a letter sent to the Assembly whereby you supported each other and expressed your loyalty to each other by asking for my decision not to be honoured or implemented?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we could call it a petition, a letter, or a decision. The gist of it is that we recommended to the deputies of the RS Assembly to ignore your decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that you were all ready to go to the trenches should Mladic be replaced? You all stated that you would leave the Main Staff but remain defending the republic, and by virtue of such act, I would have been left without a Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this has not been admitted thus far, could we admit it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it not admitted when General Milovanovic gave evidence? I think I remember having seen this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was convinced it had previously been admitted, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us move on. We'll sort it out in the meantime. Otherwise, we'll admit it later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the VRS had only some 2.000 professional officers for some 209- or 210.000 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that the 209.000 soldiers were not professional, that it was a people's army comprised of recruits and reservists, some of whom had never even served their military service?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part there were reservists. There were 14.000 reserve NCOs and 7.000 COs. The rest were military conscripts. Mr. Karadzic, we had very few recruits. The annual contingent of recruits amounted to as little as 6.000. As for the social structure of the army itself was that most people were workers or farmers. It was a great burden on the army, because people had their vocations or worked the land and wanted to work in order to support their families. It was for that reason that they frequently tried to avoid serving in the military and implement military tasks. The professionalism and education of our military ranks was a problematic issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We'll see another document created by you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I was informed that the letter, General's letter to the Assembly, was admits as Exhibit D2159.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's why I was rising, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this particular kind of structure, that is to say that people who either worked or farmed, created problems in terms of command and control, because people were not prepared to defend anything other than their land and villages? In other words, it was impossible to conduct a manoeuvre.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we have 1D5166. Unfortunately, we only have a translation of your text in the VRS from May 1992 where you address this issue of social strata or structure. Did you write such an article?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a different thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is it. In your list of documents, I'm seeing an item which is entitled "Notes of Mr. Skrbic." Seven --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 1D5170. Is that what you said, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D5165.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you the author of this text? Can we go to the next page and I'll read out the part in English which addresses the issue. Did you write this article on the occasion of the second year of existence of the Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, but I don't have the Serbian text before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But did you write this? I'll read it out to you and perhaps you'll be able to recognise if you wrote it or not, the framed par: [In English] "The social structure of fighters varied at different stages of the establishment of the corps, but it was essentially a mix of workers and farmers. This later became a moral issue in terms of fairness as to which segment of the population would be assigned the most difficult tasks, as they constituted, in fact, military duties on the front line." "As they constituted, in fact, military duties on the front line." [Interpretation] If we have the Serbian version, I'd be grateful to -- for anyone who provided it to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger has it. It is noted that it was published on May 9th of 1994, in "Srpska Vojska," but I'm not sure if Mr. Karadzic needs this in putting that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I did want the witness's comment, because the text is replete with quality analyses as to the true nature of that army. It will assist the Chamber in the distinguishing between this kind of army and the professional army which is easy to command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your text, and did you write this? Is this accurate?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. I was about to start with my answer. This is my text published in "Srpska Vojska" on the 9th of May, 1994. I found the paragraph about the social structure of fighters in the process of establishment of the 2nd Krajina Corps. However, this kind of social structure was characteristic of the entire VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have this text admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2191, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us address this issue briefly. Is it correct, General -- or did our military courts work throughout the war, and were they independent in their work in terms of any influence from the commands or other authorities? What is your knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is completely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that our documents such as the Law on the Armed Forces, the Law on Defence, and others reflect in entirety such regulations pertaining to the honouring of the Geneva Conventions, the laws and customs of war, and other such legal documents?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and one can clearly see that if the documents you listed are analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you this: Do you know of a single case in which a unit received an order amounting to the commission of a crime and that -- or that such an order was ever implemented and then later on covered up by the Main Staff or other levels of military?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no personal knowledge of such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it the position of our army and command structures that the commission of crimes was encouraged, or were they clearly against the commission of any crimes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documents show that the VRS as well as the state frequently insisted on the importance of honouring the Geneva Conventions and its annexes, as well as the laws of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you picture our command cadre which would be silent or cover up or even order, say, rape?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is purely hypothetical. However, I presume that out of the 2.000 professionals we had, no one would order such a thing, but it's not easy to assert that positively. You never know what sort of people there are around, especially in terms of rape because that was your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'm not asking you about individuals but a certain unit. Would a certain unit approve of such conduct or try and cover up such conduct? For example, organised rape.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. That is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mention was made of your meeting here, your visit to me on the 14th of July, 1995. Reference is also made to the documents that you brought with you. On the occasion of that visit, do you remember that I signed those documents without reading them? I trusted the professional services from within the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think you signed them immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the information you had, since I'm not a professional soldier, did I trust these professional services, and I never checked the things they submitted to me, nor did I have any doubts as to their professional conduct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to the field that I worked in, no, you never expressed mistrust of the domain within which I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that it was your opinion that I was not fully in favour of assisting the army? I wanted to impose certain restrictions. I wanted to restrict the scope of activity that the army had, and in that sense I obstructed the army when it came to its combativeness and when it came to the army be prepared? Did you believe that the civilian authorities, and I in particular, imposed restrictions on you mostly because of the negotiations that I was involved in but for other reason as well?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the categories you mentioned in your question, Mr. Karadzic, I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that you also objected to discipline within the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? I don't think I followed you in full. You agreed with Mr. Karadzic, and you added that Mr. Karadzic objected to the discipline with the army. Is that correct, and what did you mean, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll paraphrase what the then-president, Mr. Karadzic, said. He said in the presence of General Mladic and in my presence, General, how can you have an undisciplined army? I bear this against you. I asked General Mladic, Can I answer the president's question? General Mladic said, Please go ahead. Mr. President, I said, the army only has 2.000 professional soldiers, but there are 209.000 men, and you're comparing us to the police that has a force of 9.000 men, and they're all professionals. I don't remember what the president's answer was, but that was what was said in essence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was: What did you mean when you said Karadzic also objected to discipline within the army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That means that at a certain level orders were not obeyed. I don't know which orders the president had in mind, but our impression was that there was a certain hierarchy, a certain level of discipline. I apologise. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our impression was that there was a hierarchy and discipline up to the level of a corps. But at lower levels there was not such a level of discipline, and there were other failings such as the failings referred to in my article to an extent we could agree with the president's assessment, in fact, Your Honours, so we did agree with it. We just wanted to tell the president what the reasons were for this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It's now clear to me. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, were there other occasions on which you expressed your opinions that were contrary to mine in very strident terms, and was your opinion that this could be done without suffering any consequences? You said a minute ago that you can't remember what I answered. If my answer had been unpleasant, you would have remembered it. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether on the whole it was possible to discuss things with me openly without having to suffer any consequences?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I spoke to you quite openly, and I didn't suffer any consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 14th when you visited me, do you remember the time? Were the civilian authorities from Srebrenica and Bratunac in my office before that time or after that time? Do you know what the time was, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the document from your secretary could have reminded me of the time. Without that document, I probably would have remembered the time, but in the document it says that I saw you from 12.15 to 12.36 on the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And after that, the civilian authorities arrived, and do you agree that this is why I couldn't inform you of the fact that I would be declaring a state of war in that area, because I had no information according to which there was such a concentration of forces from the 28th Division in the woods?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course you didn't tell me anything about your intentions with regard to declaring a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the time, at the time of that meeting, was there anything said about POWs or war crimes? Was there anything that had to do with such issues in the air, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, see the time. When were you planning to have a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time now. But is it true that you encountered Mr. Deronjic or somebody from Srebrenica after your meeting is over with Mr. Karadzic at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I didn't know that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or delegation -- or did you see a delegation from Srebrenica or that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I only came to a conclusion on the basis of the document from Mr. Karadzic's secretary. Perhaps you've seen that document yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm seeing that document before me, but it says your meeting is over at 12.35, and there's a meeting at 12.40. So I was wondering whether you met any of those delegations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's a possibility. There were some people sitting in the reception area where the secretary was, but I didn't pay any attention to them, nor did I speak with them. I did what I had to do and then I left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's fair enough. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 1.00. Just a second. I'm sorry, 1.30. We'll have a break for an hour. In the meantime, there's an oral ruling I'd like to issue at this moment. With respect to the accused's request to have assistance of Defence expert in courtroom for testimony of Expert Witness Butler filed on 5th of March, 2012, which the Prosecution does not oppose, the Chamber grants the request in light of the technical nature of the evidence to be provided by Richard Butler following the past practice of the Chamber. We will resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.32 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I will try to be clear and concise in order to get yes or no answers, although I hope that the Trial Chamber's not going to interrupt us if we are efficient. We will have a topic or two left. Anyway, was it your knowledge that buses were needed for Srebrenica in order to evacuate the persons who wanted to move somewhere else of their own accord?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's not how I defined it in my statement in Popovic et al. I said for the evacuation of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know of any kind of forcible evacuation, or did it go without saying that this is what the law stipulated, that they were supposed to be evacuated from a combat area, and did they want to evacuate themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Three entirely separate questions, Mr. President, very easily confused if not made -- if not parsed out and presented to the witness individually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Could you break down your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, did you have any knowledge to the effect that this evacuation was forcible?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did it go without saying? Was it readily understood that the people being evacuated were the people who wished to be moved somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct, General, that directive number 7 was passed -- or, rather, created in a somewhat different way than usual? Namely, directives were usually created in the presence of all of you and with the participation of all of you, but you did not take part in creating this directive?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in my previous questions to such questions, I used my general military knowledge, and that is what I'd like to do now as well. As far as directive number 7 is concerned, I wouldn't want to change anything in relation to what I said in Popovic et al. and earlier on in the interview given to Mr. McCloskey on the 12th of July, 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to hear you live in this case as well, but let's move on then, and if you find if convenient, you're going to tell us about what I ask now, too. Are directives doctrinary instructions rather than strict executive orders, and do executive orders come into being only after directives have been created?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Directives are such documents. General guidelines for warfare are provided in these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If in a directive a higher instance ordered the commission of a crime wilfully or willingly or unwillingly, does the lower instance have the right to refuse that and to caution against that and ask for a change?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any action that leads to the commission of a crime is subject to such procedure, namely that that not be carried out and that one's superior officer should be informed. I think that that is what the regulations say as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that certain sentences that are contained in directive number 7 that are not quite clear or correct were not repeated in directive 7/1 that Mladic sent as the basis for carrying out executive orders?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These two directives are different. I saw them after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that at the time when these directives were being created and implemented you did not have any knowledge of their good or bad sides?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D5170. I'd like to have that called up, please. Did you take notes on the basis of intelligence that arrived in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. Take a look at these notes and tell us -- actually, first of all, tell us whether these are the said notes typed up.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. These are my personal notes that were created between the 18th of March, 1995, until sometime in May that same year. I put this annotation here. O denotes operative, and that is a compilation of intelligence that I reviewed when I went to Crna Rijeka to the main command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So these are not anyone's opinions or wishes. These are documents that could be used for writing memoirs -- or, actually, this is the essence of the documents that could have been used for writing memoirs, studies and the like; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I applied scientific methods, because I wrote my own remarks by saying prim.ps, my initials, Petar Skrbic, and the rest are the sentences that I created on the basis of intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you or writer of certain parts of certain encyclopedias, then you are familiar with that kind of writing, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 21st January -- actually, the 20th of March, 1995. Does it not say that the Muslims bought 15 rockets and that they arrived in humanitarian aid convoys? The circled part towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but that was written on the 21st of January, 1995, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I thought that it said the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something different on the 20th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That date -- that date should read 21st of March, shouldn't it? Would you like to see the next page in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in B/C/S. Exactly. It says the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you look at the 24th of March, 0.6, that is, in Zepa Muslims and Croats clashed because the Croats did not allow Mujahedin volunteers to go to Teslic. And was Teslic under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Teslic was under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And also this information that although there was an alliance, the Croats nevertheless did not allow the Mujahedin in. What do you understand Mujahedin to mean, fighters from Arab countries?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And the unit was called El Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have operative 13, OP 13 -- or, rather, O.13. I have to skip a few.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Serbian the last three digits of the ERN number are 340. Underneath these bullets or bullet points, although they're interesting, too, it says: "The assessment of the West is that inter-Serb squabbles will continue until certain officials are replaced." Do you agree that inter-Serb squabbles were something that the Muslims and the Croats and the West liked?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have O.17. In English as well, please. So on the 10th of April, on the 10th of April, you have the essence of some information stating that: "NATO is intensively reconnoitering protected areas and gathering information on Serbian features for possible bombing." Do you agree that NATO Air Force did pass this information on to the other side as well? They didn't only gather this information for themselves. And also, officers on the ground often provided information on our situation.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is de facto correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say here that you received information to the effect that "Turkey was arming Muslims and sending Mujahedin to Bosnia," right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what was written in some intelligence report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry I didn't rise earlier because this may and practice. In the last answer it's the second time the accused has elicited information or a response from the witness on information -- alleged information that was not contained in this document. The witness has indicated the basis for the -- his preparation for this document, at least to modest extent, but now suddenly we're entering into areas that we don't know anything about the provenance of the information. So if that could be provided, I won't have to spend as much time in redirect asking about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you understand the question of Mr. Tieger? When you agreed with the suggestion of Mr. Karadzic that NATO Air Force passed this kind of information on to the Bosnian side, what is your basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood Mr. Tieger's question very well. The basis is an intelligence report from which this information is derived. Secondly, my personal experience shows what this reconnaissance was like. In Western Bosnia, I saw NATO reconnaissance aircraft and their flights. So the information was fully confirmed in practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question was whether NATO gave this information to Bosnian authorities. How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of all the activities that were undertaken by the Croatian Army and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina vis-a-vis us. They knew exactly, Your Honours, where our artillery was deployed, where the refugees were. They knew the deployment of our forces. They could not have established that on the basis of the resources they had. That could only have come from intelligence that they had received by way of electronic surveillance or aerial images.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the kind of answer I expected. Please go on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the last box it says -- or the date is the 10th of April: [As read] "NATO aviation is -- the Muslims are doing similar things in order to get NATO support, the support of NATO aircraft." General, was it certain that the provocations they engaged in were provocations, the purpose of which was to get NATO involved in the war? I'm referring to the English page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says that they are moving along all the axis of Majevica and Vlasic, and in this boxed-in part there's information according to which they are doing similar things in the protected zones and the objective is to provoke the Serbs and to make sure that NATO gets involved; is that correct? And was that something that was always clear to us?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the army this was always completely clear to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can keep the English version there. Could we see the following page in the Serbian version. It says, in the Sarajevo area there was provocative action and the purpose was yet again the same, to gain the sympathy of the international community and to ensure that NATO took action against the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we see O.22, please. It's the 15th of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, April 1995. I apologise. At the top it says, it's not in a box, in Rukavica [phoen] area, the Muslims brought in the Black Swans. Were the Black Swans a well-known paramilitary formation that was subsequently part of the ABiH? I don't know how it's been translated. The Black Swans.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a paramilitary unit. They had various sorts of formations with various names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again it says there were provocations to make sure that the Serbs responded to the provocations. Could we scroll up. Could we scroll up the page in the Serbian version. In the English it says they're moving out the population from parts of the town and they killed a French soldier and they opened fire on a Russian soldier. Was this interpreted by us as a preparations for some kind of an offensive?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Moving out the population reveals for any officer who is trained or not so trained that intensive combat is being prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see O.25 now. This is something from Gorazde, but Gorazde isn't in the indictment, so I don't want to waste time on that. There's information provided on the 5th of May. An action on the 30th of May. Two thousand Serbs were killed in Western Slavonia. Did we subsequently find out that more than 2.000 were, in fact, killed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's not information that I was provided. It's information from intelligence reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you put another question. Not only were Serbs killed, but about 500- to 600.000 people from territory were moved out. Serbs, in the course of the war, they created many problems for us, for the army, when it came to feeding them and you complained that we couldn't even feed our troops let alone refugees. There was a column of refugees of Bijeljina to Petrovac and Drvar. They covered a distance of 600 kilometres man to man, horse by horse, the elderly were pushing carts. These were refugees from Croatia and then there were refugees from the western parts of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. O.35, please. It says that -- well, the date is the 15th. It says that Izetbegovic on the 12th of May took a decision on carrying out an operation to raise the blockade of Sarajevo. The purpose was to take Ilidza, Hadzici, Ilijas and to launch an attack from the external part and internal part of that sector, of that ring.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the text says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we see the following page, O.36. Do we agree that this concerns the 1st Corps? Do you agree that in Lukavica, Vojkovici, Pavlovac and Linjaca [phoen], the population was a hundred per cent Serbian and these settlements were civilian ones?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, Mr. Karadzic. These places were inhabited by civilians, but I don't know what the ethnic composition was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If they'd broken through our lines would the inhabitants there have come to harm given what you know about the action that they would take?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are assumptions but quite realistic ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you confirm for the benefit of the Chamber that these are places in the Serbian part of Sarajevo, and they are an integral part of what was once a unified town?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I presume we're talking about the excerpts that were referenced and to those I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I had time, I'd ask that the entire document be admitted. It would be useful for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How would it be useful?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, it will give you an overview of the intelligence that arrived in the Main Staff, the intelligence that guided the Main Staff when they decided on action to be taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It may not be necessary for me to rise, but I'd make two very obvious points. First, it's completely contrary to the practice that's been instituted and followed in this Chamber, and number two, this is not the intelligence that arrived at the Main Staff. At best this is a selective portion of that that the witness undertook to write in his -- in this particular document. So it doesn't even serve the purpose the accused suggests, even if the practice was permitted as we have in the past, and of course the -- there are any number of documents the Prosecution would have been and remains happy to produce in their entirety under this rationale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Without seeing them, we can't find whether it's relevant or not. Let's follow our practice, Mr. Karadzic. That is to say, if necessary, some parts can be added, if necessary at all. I'm sorry. We'll admit only those passages [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] I only wanted the witness to confirm whether it's true that this comes from intelligence that you gathered in the Main Staff, intelligence that the Main Staff had at its disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has given his ruling. We'll give the number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2192, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D5164.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you remember this daily report of yours that you sent as the assistant commander in the 2nd Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And does it say here -- well, the first paragraph speaks about the negotiations that were broken off in Geneva, and the second paragraph says that according to initial information, our participation in the commission for investigating the massacre in Sarajevo was accepted. Do you remember that the massacre was used as a reason to break off these negotiations in Geneva? Do you remember that initially they accepted that our investigators should participate in investigation of this incident, and subsequently they rejected this possibility?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the basis of that information that I compiled this report, which I forwarded to the subordinate units in the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2193, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me first ask you, General, is it correct that Muslim and Croatian parents prevented their children from going to serve in the JNA in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In 1991, that was not a phenomenon that was that [indiscernible] present, but in 1992, they tried to prevent them from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was that the position of the political leadership of those communities as well?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially the leaderships you have referred to made an appeal and asked them not to join the army, and later they issued orders according to which the JNA should not be joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we see 1D5167. General, do we agree that these very same parents, in March 1995, sent their children to do their military service, and you issued an order stating that their training should be provided in Manjaca? Can you confirm that? Can you tell us why it was better for them to be in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, because the training centre of the Main Staff of the VRS was in Manjaca. Manjaca is a place next to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we scroll up the English version. Did you also think that it would be nicer for them if they were together? It was better to provide them with food in accordance with their religion. It was better for them to be together.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2194, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that you have three minutes left, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there was an important document I wanted to call up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not acceptable, Mr. Karadzic. You have spent almost an hour on just marginally relevant background matters, and at the end of session you say you have important document. In order to correct that -- the practice, we will not allow you any extended time. Please continue. You have three minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, perhaps you could answer by saying yes or no, but do you remember that at a meeting of the Supreme Command on the 31st of March, 1995, freedom of movement was discussed? And would you agree that on that occasion our position was reiterated, our position according to which no one should be forced to stay behind or to leave? And I'm referring to civilians.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do you know whether we ever had the intention to separate from Muslims who were living in Republika Srpska? Did we ever want to drive out the Muslims and the Croats from territory that would be part of the constituent Serbian entity?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have said that the Muslims lived there in the same manner as other citizens from Republika Srpska under difficult wartime conditions. It was in Prijedor, Banja Luka, Mrkonjic Grad, Sanski Most, and so on and so forth. They lived in these places in a very normal way. When the Croatian Army attacked Mrkonjic Grad with their artillery, the Muslims and Serbs were both shelled. I was personally present on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Did anyone at any time - I'm referring to those officials - have the position according to which the Muslims and Croats should be destroyed in part or in their entirety? Was it their position that they should be killed and destroyed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard anyone ever put things in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know how our army would bury enemy soldiers? For example, from a certain zone Oric lost 2.000 soldiers in our areas. Do you know how our army would bury these soldiers once the battles were over?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know, Mr. Karadzic. The sector for the rear was responsible for dealing with such matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. Sorry for rushing through, but I wanted to gain your insight both from the level of your federal ministry and elsewhere, and as I was trying to go -- move things along, I may have rushed you, but thank you in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger. Do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, today at page 23, Mr. Karadzic asked you about praising General Krstic, and you recalled comments from Mr. Karadzic regarding General Mladic becoming a living legend because we turned him into one, but there were other generals who needed to take praise, including General Krstic. I wondered if you quoted Mr. Karadzic precisely, indicated it might be a paraphrase. If -- in that connection could we turn to -- please to 65 ter 45049A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, it is Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, it's not federation -- oh, yes. Now it was corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, are those the comments to which you referred earlier and that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd move that into admission, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give the date of it again? August something.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe it's the 4th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P4555, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be fair to -- to put the question to the General about the context, and the date is the 4th, and what the decision that was made was, whether it had anything to do with Mladic's dismissal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think Mr. Karadzic's examination is completed, and I'd appreciate the opportunity to complete mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, we saw the comments in the video. Did you know that General Krstic planned the Srebrenica operation in front of Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I found that out after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, next I want to turn to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After the war how, General? Could you tell us what you heard about the planning of that operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not about the planning of the operation, but I learned of this footage that Mr. Kosta Cavoski commented upon in his book. I read his book, and that's how I know what Mr. Karadzic had stated, and I paraphrased him here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will leave it at that. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, at page 42 earlier, Mr. Karadzic asked you about genocide -- the genocide of World War II and his own involvement in inciting or manipulating the Serb people with those memories, and you said in your response that you -- no person -- you just wanted to answer the thesis of genocide and indicated that: "No person, including Karadzic or Raskovic or anyone, needed to tell the people of the dangers of genocide. The Serb people were well aware of it." But, in fact, General, is it correct or not that the SDS took steps to ensure that the Serb people were reminded of the genocide and to credit for reminding the Serb people of the genocide in order to warn them about the alleged illusions of living together?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm asking the question as a foundation first, and I'll follow up if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, if you could answer the question.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the interpretation I received is "SPS," which is short for the Socialist Party of Serbia, but in English it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me clarify then. It's SDS, Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, Mr. Tieger. Yes, I can see it in the transcript in English. All those political parties, Mr. Tieger, act politically. They tried to remind people of different things, and I do not exclude this possibility that the SDS reminded the people of the genocide, but my point was that the people didn't need much explanation to realise that quite realistic danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn then to 65 ter 11934, please. And if we could turn to the second page in B/C/S. And, General, if you'd look at the first column to the left, the second-to-last or third-to-last full paragraph on that column. And you'll see the following reference from Mr. Velibor Ostojic, who served as the minister of information of, among other things, for Republika Srpska for a long period, saying: "The next task initiated at that time as well was to remind of the tragic events from recent Serbian history and to excavate from the pits the bones of Serbs so atrociously killed during World War II. It was a warning about illusions of living together with the enemy which had been accepted by the Serbian people. The Serbian people suddenly realised that they had been deceived and misled and that its recent history full of tragedy, genocide, exodus and disenfranchisement had been concealed." And then if we look at the second column at the bottom of that, we see references by Mr. Ostojic to the success and crucial tasks of the SDS, including preparing the Serbian people for defence so that they would be prepared. And then moving on to the next page, again asserting -- asserting --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask Mr. Tieger not to paraphrase but to directly quote Mr. Ostojic so that we see what it is all about really.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "The SDS was preparing the defence of the Serbian people, and it was also preparing them in a national manner. Therefore, the Serbian people were more prepared than their enemy for the first time in their modern history." And finally moving on to the top of the next-to-last column: "So these are the two greatest achievements of the SDS and they are only the first stage towards the final goal, unification of the Serbian nation." So, General, is that a reflection of the fact that despite your view that the Serbian people didn't need to be reminded of that, that the SDS took the position that they did need to be reminded of the genocide of World War II in order to ensure that people abandoned the idea that they could live together?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Could you reformulate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, do you see this article as being a reflection of SDS efforts to remind people for the reasons stated, or do you see this article as reflecting some other aspects of efforts by the SDS as related by Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you noticed well that we have an interview with Mr. Velibor Ostojic as part of this article. I don't know whether he was in the seat of a minister at the time or not, but this was his position. He does indicate what you mentioned. I cannot dispute his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I tender this, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think I read the English part you read out. Where did you read it from? Can you help me find the passage? Unification ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You are correct. The unification appears at the top of the third column. That part wasn't translated. I'm aware of that -- that translation. If we can either just -- and I think the witness confirmed it. I can have that brief portion translated and added to the excerpted translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But was it not our practice not to admit third party's interviews? Is it not an interview statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is an interviewer's statement. It reflects directly on the position put by the accused. He is an official of the SDS party relating the official position of the party at a time both throughout the passage of that. I think it's a different matter and should be admitted, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't think you have to worry about that, because the witness didn't do anything other than say what is in the article. He didn't confirm anything about it, so I don't think it's admissible through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's -- that -- excuse me for interrupting. First of all, two things, Mr. President. This passes the test earlier. It's a contemporaneous statement by the witness. That's a marker that the Defence placed on admission of such documents when it attempted to introduce them itself. And secondly, the witness has both contextualised it. It was raised by the -- by the accused. Now the Prosecution's responding to it to put further illumination on something that's already been contextualised. It really would be inappropriate not to admit this, and it would be running from information elicited, basically, by comments and questions from the accused and now provide further amplification by the Prosecution in its redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Chamber is minded to stick to our previous practice given that this is a third party's interview given to a media which was called "Javnost," and all the witness confirmed is that since such interview existed, and to the extent the witness confirmed, that's already in our evidence. We'll not admit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I -- I would like to be heard on it further, but I don't want to be arguing against the Court's ruling, but I -- if the Court wanted to hear why this is appropriate, I could amplify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I think we -- I thought we heard from you, but let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You'll have another opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I only have one more questions but I want to make sure I understand this right. We saw the accused discuss with you at length your access to and recording of highly sensitive intelligence information, at least information that you asserted came from that source during the period of April and May 1995, which reflected activities in a variety of spheres. Did you have the same access to information in June and July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tieger. On the 25th of May, I stopped and no longer kept such information, because I was busy with other tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So on the basis -- this information allowed you to know how many Serbs were allegedly killed in Slavonia, but without it you, as I understand it, were unaware of anything that happened in Srebrenica until you heard it from the media. Is that basically the situation as you describe it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, information I received as intelligence information had to do with the period between March and May 1995 and no other period, in particular the other period you pointed out. Information about those killed in Western Slavonia is not something I made up. I copied it from intelligence reports. I can neither confirm nor deny its accuracy. That's what the reports stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Mr. President. I -- if the Court wishes, again I don't mean to chafe under a previous ruling, but I do think I'd ask the Court to take another look at the contemporaneous statement Rule -- practices that we followed that I think Mr. Robinson forgot. Other than that, nothing further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, today on transcript page 13, lines 12 to 15, while explaining to us why you have difficulty remembering what happened with respect to Srebrenica, you said as follows: "Your Honours, I would like to point out a methodological problem. Over these past few days and ever since the war ended, I've learned a lot more about Srebrenica than I knew at the time. I also studied some documents in the meantime, too." So I was wondering what the result of your study was, what you -- what is that you learnt a lot more about it. Could you tell us about your understanding as to how all those killings took place and who ordered it? Could you help us in that regard?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think anyone ordered the killings. However, I do not deny that they came about. I saw some footage which you probably saw, too. I saw what was being transported by the buses. Sometimes such footage was broadcast on TV as well, and you can find it on the internet. I did not prepare myself to write a scientific article about it, so my observations were for my personal use and insight only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what was your personal observation at the end of the day, General?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression was that indeed the population was evacuated but that they were offered to stay, too. A Muslim delegation signed an agreement in the presence of Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans that they would all move under the auspices of the UN. That is the information I had. Then I watched some video footage on the internet and elsewhere on how those columns of buses left Potocari for Kladovo and other places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, General Skrbic. On behalf of the Tribunal, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I leave it to you whether to start with the next witness or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It will be Mr. Nicholls. Let me see what his view is on that and if I can just have one minute. Thanks, Mr. President. It seems like your sense was -- was shared, and I think it would be probably more appropriate under the circumstances just to commence on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Given that we had some longer days sometime during the week, I think it's better to adjourn for the week unless there are any other matters to raise at the moment. The hearing is adjourned. We will resume on Monday - in the morning or in the afternoon. I have to check - at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 12th day of March, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.35 p.m.,
